subtitle: Relationships: phrasal verbs, dilemmas and difficult conversations

3.1: Use these expressions: complete the sentences

slides.title: Behind Closed Doors
slides.question: Relationships · Warm-up
slides.summary: A warm-up about relationships: someone who stops replying without explaining why, two people who care about each other but are bad for each other, people who stay in unhappy relationships, and staying out of loyalty.

expressions.meaning: talk to someone directly about a problem.
accept what happened and continue with your life.
really care about someone, honestly.
because you feel you must be loyal.

items.question: Someone stops replying to your messages without explaining why. Would you confront them or simply move on?
blocks: because I'd rather know the truth
items.explain: I'd rather… than… compares two options.

items.question: Can two people genuinely care about each other but still be bad for each other?
items.explain: bring out the worst in someone = make someone behave badly.

gloss.pt: se importar de verdade com alguém

gloss.en: bring out the worst in someone

items.question: Why do people sometimes stay in relationships they are clearly unhappy with?
blocks: out of fear of being alone
items.explain: out of fear of + -ING: out of fear of being alone.

items.question: Should we maintain relationships out of loyalty, even when they no longer make us happy?
blocks: but staying only out of loyalty
items.explain: in the long run = after a long time.

slides.title: When Relationships Change
slides.question: Phrasal verbs in context · B2–C1
slides.summary: Six phrasal verbs about how relationships change: friends who drift apart after moving, people who fall out over something stupid, who patch things up, someone who bottles everything up, someone who finally opens up, and someone who puts up with constant criticism.

expressions.meaning: slowly become less close to someone.
stop being friends after an argument.
make peace after an argument.
keep your feelings inside instead of expressing them.
start talking honestly about your feelings.
accept something annoying without complaining.

items.question: Can you guess the meaning of each bold expression from its context?
items.explain: Guessing from context is a key B2–C1 skill.

items.question: Which expressions describe a temporary situation, and which might describe a long-term change?
items.explain: Gerunds as subjects: Falling out is…, drifting apart is…

items.question: Which of these situations have you witnessed in real life?
items.explain: see someone + verb: I've seen two friends drift apart.

slides.title: What Would You Say?
slides.question: Active vocabulary · Choose & justify
slides.summary: Choose the right phrasal verb for six situations. Then think beyond the answer: which situations could seriously damage a relationship, which problems can be solved, and have you experienced one? Advanced challenge: explain why your phrasal verb fits better than another.

expressions.meaning: slowly become less close to someone.
stop being friends after an argument.
make peace after an argument.
keep your feelings inside instead of expressing them.
start talking honestly about your feelings.
accept something annoying without complaining.

items.question: Which of these situations could seriously damage a relationship?
items.explain: put up with + noun; -ING form as subject.

items.question: Which of these problems can be solved, and which might be irreversible?
items.explain: can be solved = passive voice.

items.question: Have you ever experienced a situation similar to one of these?
blocks: to open up to my friends.
items.explain: used to = a past habit. open up TO someone.

slides.title: The Relationship Crossroads
slides.question: Real-life dilemmas · Critical thinking
slides.summary: Three real-life dilemmas: a one-sided friendship (your best friend only contacts you when they need something), love vs. self-respect (someone puts up with criticism and controlling behavior), and family expectations (your family disapproves of your partner). Use at least two expressions when defending your opinion.

expressions.meaning: set a limit you will not accept beyond.
defend yourself and your rights.
pretend not to see something wrong.
slowly accept a difficult situation.
do something good to compensate for something bad.
leave a situation or a relationship.

items.question: The one-sided friendship: Would you confront them, distance yourself, or end the friendship?
blocks: I would talk to them first,
items.explain: Second conditional: if nothing changed, I would…

items.question: How many chances should someone get?
blocks: Two or three chances are fair,
you have to draw the line.
items.explain: at some point = eventually.

items.question: Love vs. self-respect: Can love justify tolerating certain behaviors?
items.explain: justify + -ING: justify turning…

items.question: When does compromise become a lack of self-respect?
items.explain: stop + -ING = no longer do it.

items.question: Family expectations: Should family opinions influence your romantic decisions?
blocks: come to terms with my choice.
items.explain: come to terms WITH something.

items.question: Would you go against your family's wishes to be with someone you love?
items.explain: make up FOR something = compensate.

slides.title: The Conversation You've Been Avoiding
slides.question: Advanced roleplay · 10 minutes
slides.summary: You've been close friends for years, but something has changed: your friend only contacts you when they need help, rarely asks how you're doing and gets defensive when you bring it up. You're the frustrated friend; your teacher plays the defensive friend.

expressions.en: I don't want to sound harsh, but…
expressions.meaning: softens a criticism before you say it.
brings the conversation back to the real issue.

expressions.en: I get where you're coming from.
expressions.meaning: I understand your point of view.
it has been worrying me for a while.

expressions.en: I can't keep pretending everything is fine.
expressions.meaning: I can't act as if nothing is wrong.

expressions.en: Where do we go from here?
expressions.meaning: what do we do now?

items.question: Explain what's been bothering you.
blocks: I don't want to sound harsh, but
items.explain: Start softly, then say the problem directly.
hl: I don't want to sound harsh, but

gloss.en: I don't want to sound harsh, but…

items.question: Give a specific example.
blocks: how my new job was going.
items.explain: "didn't even" stresses that it was the minimum.

items.question: Your friend says: "I've just been really busy lately."
blocks: I get where you're coming from,
but it's been weighing on me
items.explain: Accept their point, then explain your feeling.
hl: I get where you're coming from

gloss.en: I get where you're coming from

items.question: Your friend says: "You're making this bigger than it actually is."
items.explain: keep + -ING: keep pretending.
hl: I can't keep pretending everything is fine.

gloss.en: I can't keep pretending everything is fine.
gloss.pt: não dá mais para fingir que está tudo bem

items.question: Make your expectations clear.
blocks: and really listen to the answer.
items.explain: need someone TO do something.

items.question: Decide whether this friendship is worth saving.
blocks: where do we go from here?
items.explain: A good way to move from the problem to a solution.
hl: where do we go from here?

gloss.en: Where do we go from here?

slides.title: The Uncomfortable Truth
slides.question: Final speaking challenge · 2–3 minutes
slides.summary: Are we becoming less tolerant in relationships, or simply learning not to accept things we once put up with? Give a clear opinion, two arguments, a real-life example and an opposing view, and finish strongly. Use at least four expressions. No script, no reading.

expressions.meaning: slowly become less close to someone.
stop being friends after an argument.
keep your feelings inside.
start talking honestly about your feelings.
set a limit you will not accept beyond.
defend yourself and your rights.
leave a situation or a relationship.
slowly accept a difficult situation.

items.question: The big question: Are we becoming less tolerant in relationships, or are we simply learning not to accept things we once put up with?
items.explain: draw the line AT something.

items.question: Have people become too quick to walk away from relationships?
items.explain: too quick TO do something.

items.question: Is protecting your peace sometimes just an excuse to avoid difficult conversations?
items.explain: Gerunds as subjects and after "than".

items.question: Are modern relationships becoming more conditional?
blocks: people stand up for themselves more,
items.explain: stand up for THEMSELVES (plural).

items.question: Final teacher challenge: What if you're the person someone else decides to walk away from? Would you still feel the same way?
items.explain: eventually = in the end, after some time (not "eventualmente").

writing.prompt: Advanced Challenge: don't just give the answer. Explain why your chosen phrasal verb fits the situation better than another expression.
checklist: Choose one sentence from the exercise
Explain what the phrasal verb means in that context
Compare it with another expression from the list
writing.model: In sentence 3, "drift apart" fits better than "fall out" because there was no argument. The two people simply had less and less in common, so the change was slow and natural, not sudden.

checklist: Consider the opposite point of view
Use at least TWO phrasal verbs
writing.model: I'd choose the one-sided friendship. First, I would confront my friend and explain how I feel. If nothing changed, I would draw the line and walk away from the friendship, because a friendship should go both ways and I need to stand up for myself. On the other hand, my friend might be going through a hard time, so I would give them one more chance.
